va_hkl_east.blurb: The eastern half of a large Appalachian massif in the far southwest corner of Virginia, spread across Wise and Scott counties. This is mainly a bouldering destination on hard sandstone blocks. The Labyrinth, a tightly packed boulderfield on the ridgeline above a reservoir, holds the most problems, with Flag Rock, Osborne Rock/Ridge and Clear Creek making up much of the rest. Many blocks there have flat landings, and some are tall enough for highballs while others are low and easy. Problems run from the easiest grades to about V8, with the bulk in the V1 to V4 range. A smaller group of sport routes spans roughly 5.8 to 5.12, with a few trad lines.

wa_tum_tum.blurb: About thirty miles northwest of Spokane, Tum Tum is a cluster of dark granite slabs and domes close to the road, with trails leading to smaller, higher domes. The rock is solid, and the climbing leans on slabs, faces and cracks. Sport routes make up most of the climbing, with a smaller share of trad, some multi-pitch lines, and a handful of boulders. Most roped climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.11, with the greatest number around 5.10, and a few reach 5.12 and 5.13. Larger crags include Banana Split Dome, Infinity Wall, Little Matterhorn Rock and Twin Pines Buttress. Rattlesnakes and poison ivy are both worth watching for.

co_guanella_pass.blurb: A high-elevation bouldering area south of Georgetown, with sub-alpine boulders scattered along the road up the pass at roughly 10,400 feet. It works as a day trip from the Denver and Golden side, and walks to the blocks are short. Everything here is bouldering, and the grade spread is unusually deep: a solid base of V0 to V4, plenty in the V5 to V8 range, and a notable number of problems at V10 and above. The biggest clusters are the 7 Mile Boulders and the Subspace Boulders, followed by the Ice Knife Area and Dark Horse Boulder. Many of the best problems were developed in recent years.

nm_el_rito.blurb: A conglomerate venue in northern New Mexico, set in the high country around 7,000 to 7,600 feet near the village of El Rito. The rock is a mass of cobbles in a sandstone matrix, so pockets and pullable cobbles define the climbing. Sport routes dominate, mostly between 5.9 and 5.12 with the greatest number at 5.10, plus some easier ground and a few 5.13s. The Traditional Area offers moderate two-pitch lines up to about 200 feet, and Little River Wall is a rock fin beside the river with mostly moderate routes. A small amount of bouldering rounds it out. Wind can be strong at the sport crags.

ny_long_island.blurb: Not a single crag but a scattering of bouldering sites across the northern side of Suffolk County, from Manhasset in the west out to East Marion on the North Fork. The climbing is all bouldering, on blocks left behind when glaciers retreated. Many sit in scenic coastal or wooded settings, and a few are affected by the tide. The grades run from V0 into the low double digits, with most problems between V0 and V3 and a thinner tail of harder ones. Split Rock, East Marion Boulders, Wildwood State Park and Duck Pond Point are the largest groups. Wildwood centers on a big boulder on a wooded bluff above Long Island Sound.

or_rocky_butte.blurb: An urban crag on an extinct volcanic cinder cone in northeast Portland beside Interstate 205, about fifteen minutes from downtown. The basalt walls are short, mostly 30 to 35 feet, and trad climbing makes up the largest share, followed by top-rope and sport, with a little bouldering. Most climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.11, with the heaviest concentration at 5.10 and 5.11, and a few go to 5.12 and 5.13. Wall of Shadows is the largest section, alongside Toothpick Wall, Silver Bullet Bluff and Video Bluff. Trees shade the rock, which helps on hot days, but it stays damp in the rainy season and is climbable much of the rest of the year. Expect a noisy, somewhat overgrown setting.
